848.title: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight
848.hook: the war is won, the teacher raises his plough at the winner, and flowers fall on the man who lost
848.carry: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight
848.howItsDone: The mace fight and its aftermath are told in recitations and retellings of the Mahabharata, and some retellings give Duryodhana a measure of honor in defeat.

segments.voice: Your line: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight. Yesterday Arjuna struck his own thigh, and Bhima's blow broke Duryodhana's. What signal did you catch yourself giving without a word? Day eight hundred forty-eight.

Duryodhana lies on the ground and can't get up. The fight is over. The Pandavas have won the war. And for a moment, nobody behaves the way winners are supposed to. Bhima walks over to the fallen king and puts his foot on his head. Yudhishthira, his own brother, tells him to stop. And Balarama, the teacher who trained both fighters, is so angry at the blow he just saw that he lifts his plough, his own weapon, and runs at Bhima. Today, the moments right after the last duel, when the victory itself is put on trial.
screen: `THE KING CAN'T RISE.` → `A FOOT ON HIS HEAD.` → `THE TEACHER CHARGES.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira speaks first. In Ganguli's telling he tells Bhima that this man is a king, and their kinsman, and that his foot does him no honor. Then Krishna catches hold of Balarama before he reaches Bhima. He reminds him of Bhima's vow, made in the dice hall, and of the wrongs done to the Pandavas. Balarama isn't persuaded. He says, in effect, that Bhima will be remembered as a crooked fighter, and he leaves for Dvaraka in anger. So the teacher of both men walks away from the winner. Then the fallen king speaks. Duryodhana, unable to stand, turns on Krishna and lists the deaths he calls unfair: Bhishma behind Shikhandi, Drona and the false news about his son, Karna with his wheel stuck in the earth. Krishna answers him with a list of his own: the poison, the house of lac, the dice, Draupadi dragged into the hall. Your own wrongs brought you here, he says. And Duryodhana answers that he lived as a king should, ruled, gave, fought, and now goes to heaven with his friends. Then the text does something strange. Flowers rain down from the sky on Duryodhana, and music sounds, and the Pandavas stand there downcast. Krishna tells them plainly that these warriors could not have been killed in a fair fight, and that what was done was done for them. The epic doesn't settle the argument. It lets the winner, the loser and the teacher each speak, and lets the flowers fall where they fall.
screen: `YUDHISHTHIRA REBUKES BHIMA` · `BALARAMA LEAVES IN ANGER` · `TWO LISTS OF WRONGS` · then, large: `FLOWERS ON THE LOSER`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your shoulders come down. Bring to mind an argument where you were sure you were right. Now let the other person speak in your mind, just once, as fairly as you can make them. Breathe in, and hear their side. Breathe out, and let your own side rest for a moment without defending it. You don't have to change your mind. Only let both voices be in the room. If you pray, you can bring them both to your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Shalya. The war's last book ends with a fallen king, an angry teacher, two lists of wrongs, and flowers falling from the sky.

Your line: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight. Today, when you win something, notice who isn't celebrating, and ask why. Tomorrow, night falls on the camp: Sauptika. Day eight hundred forty-eight.

849.title: Sauptika: the night massacre
849.hook: three men are all that's left of an army, and a dying king makes one of them its commander
849.howItsDone: Sauptika, from a Sanskrit word for sleep, is the name of the tenth of the Mahabharata's eighteen books, and reciters of the whole epic carry the story straight on from the fallen king into the night raid.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Shalya, the war's last day: Balarama's anger, two lists of wrongs, and flowers falling on the man who lost. Did you notice who wasn't celebrating? Today a new book opens. Day eight hundred forty-nine.

Evening on the battlefield. Three warriors come looking for their king. Ashvatthama, the son of Drona. Kripa, the old teacher of the princes. Kritavarma, a fighter from Krishna's own clan who fought on the other side. They're the last of the Kaurava army still standing. They find Duryodhana where Bhima left him, on the ground, his thighs broken, covered in dust, unable to rise. The man who once commanded a vast host now has three men and a darkening sky. Today, the start of Sauptika, the book of the night, and the strange ceremony held beside a dying king.
screen: `THREE WARRIORS LEFT.` → `THEY FIND THEIR KING.` → `THE BOOK OF THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: In Ganguli's telling, the three weep at the sight of him. Duryodhana, in pain, still speaks like a king. He tells them not to grieve, that he fought and didn't turn his back, and that this is the way of the world. But Ashvatthama can't let it rest. His grief runs into something older. He remembers how his own father, Drona, died: told a lie about his son's death, laying down his weapons, and then killed. Now he sees his king broken by a blow below the waist. He makes a vow before Duryodhana, in effect: before this night is over, I'll send the Panchalas to the land of the dead. Hear what Duryodhana does next. He can't stand. He has no army. And he asks Kripa to bring a pot of water. With that water, lying in the dust, he has Kripa install Ashvatthama as commander of the army. Of what army? Of three men. The ceremony is real to them anyway. Ashvatthama embraces the king, and the three go off into the night, and Duryodhana is left alone on the field. It's a small scene, almost quiet, but everything in this book grows out of it. A vow made in grief. A title given by a man who has nothing left to give. And a commander with no one to lead but two companions and his own anger.
screen: `THEY WEEP OVER THE KING` · `DRONA'S DEATH REMEMBERED` · `ASHVATTHAMA'S VOW` · then, large: `A COMMANDER OF THREE`

segments.voice: Sit quietly and let the evening of the story settle around you. Bring to mind a time when grief or hurt made you want to promise something big. Breathe in, and feel where that heat sits in your body: the chest, the jaw, the hands. Breathe out, and let the heat cool a little, without pushing it away. Nothing has to be decided now. Just notice how fast a sorrow can turn into a vow. If you pray, you can rest that sorrow in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Sauptika. The book of the night: three survivors, a broken king, a vow, and a commander made with a pot of water.

850.title: Sauptika: the night massacre
850.hook: two men sleep under a banyan tree, and the third lies awake watching an owl hunt
850.howItsDone: The owl among the crows appears in retellings and illustrated editions of the Mahabharata when they tell the night raid.

segments.voice: Your line: Sauptika: the night massacre. Yesterday a dying king made Ashvatthama commander of an army of three. Did you catch a hurt turning into a promise? Day eight hundred fifty.

A huge banyan tree in a forest at night, its branches full of sleeping crows. Under it, three tired warriors have stopped to rest. They've ridden away from the field, afraid the Pandavas might find them. Kripa lies down and sleeps. Kritavarma sleeps too. They're worn out, and they've been fighting for days. But Ashvatthama can't sleep. He lies on the ground with his eyes open, burning, the text says, with anger and grief. And up in the branches, something moves. Today, what one sleepless man sees in a tree, and what he decides it means.
screen: `A BANYAN FULL OF CROWS.` → `TWO MEN SLEEP.` → `ONE LIES AWAKE.`

segments.voice: In Ganguli's telling, an owl comes down through the dark. It's large and fierce, with sharp talons, and it lands among the crows while they sleep. One by one, it kills them. The crows don't wake in time to fly. By the end, the ground under the tree is scattered with their bodies, and the owl sits there, pleased with its night's work. Ashvatthama watches the whole thing. And he says to himself, in effect: this owl has taught me something. The Pandavas can't be beaten in open battle. They've won. They're strong, and they have Krishna. But they'll be asleep tonight, tired and celebrating. I can do what the owl did. Notice what the epic is doing here. Nobody gives Ashvatthama the idea. No god speaks, no adviser plots. He finds it in a tree, at the hour when he should be resting, with his companions asleep beside him. A sleepless mind reads a lesson into whatever it sees. The owl only hunted. It was Ashvatthama who made it a plan. And because his companions are asleep, there's no one awake to say it back to him and hear how it sounds. That's the hinge of the whole night. It starts as grief and anger. Under the banyan, it becomes a method.
screen: `THE OWL AMONG THE CROWS` · `THE CROWS NEVER WAKE` · `"THE OWL HAS TAUGHT ME"` · then, large: `GRIEF BECOMES A PLAN`

segments.voice: Let your body settle the way it would before sleep: shoulders heavy, jaw loose, eyes soft or closed. Bring to mind a thought that has kept you awake. Don't solve it. Breathe in, and notice it. Breathe out, and say to yourself that this can wait for morning, when others are awake. Let the next breath be slower than the last. If you pray, you can hand the thought over in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Sauptika. The night book: a banyan, sleeping crows, an owl, and one man awake who decides the owl was a lesson.
Your line: Sauptika: the night massacre. Today, if a big idea comes to you late at night, say it out loud to someone in daylight before you act on it. Day eight hundred fifty.

851.title: Sauptika: the night massacre
851.hook: an old teacher is shaken awake in the dark and told the plan, and he tries to talk his nephew out of it
851.howItsDone: Kripa's counsel under the banyan, with its talk of fate and human effort working together, is a passage some readers return to when they think about fate and action in the Mahabharata.

segments.voice: Your line: Sauptika: the night massacre. Yesterday Ashvatthama lay awake under the banyan and watched an owl kill the sleeping crows. Did a late-night idea wait for daylight? Day eight hundred fifty-one.

Kripa opens his eyes. It's still dark. His nephew is standing over him, and so is Kritavarma, who's been woken too. Ashvatthama tells them what he saw in the tree and what he means to do: go to the Pandava camp tonight, while everyone sleeps, and kill the men who killed his father. Kripa is old. He taught the princes on both sides when they were boys. He has fought this whole war beside Duryodhana. And now, half awake under a banyan, he has a few minutes to change his nephew's mind. Today, Kripa's counsel, and what happens to good advice at night.
screen: `KRIPA IS WOKEN.` → `THE PLAN IS SPOKEN.` → `A FEW MINUTES TO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Kripa doesn't shout. In Ganguli's telling he starts with an idea: success needs two things together, what fate gives and what a person does. Effort alone isn't enough, and neither is fate. Then he gets practical. Don't decide this alone, he says, in effect. Let's go to Dhritarashtra, to Gandhari, to the wise Vidura, and ask them what should be done. And he names the thing directly: killing men who are asleep is not honored in this world. Ashvatthama listens, and he has an answer for everything. The Panchalas broke the rules first, he says. Dhrishtadyumna killed my father while he sat with his weapons laid down. Bhima struck the king below the waist. Why should I keep rules they didn't? He says he cannot sleep while they live. He even says, in effect, that he doesn't care if he's reborn as a worm or an insect for it. Then he yokes his horses and drives off toward the camp. And here is the quiet turn. Kripa and Kritavarma don't go home. They don't warn anyone. They get up and follow him. Kripa gave the right counsel, clearly, kindly, with a better plan. It wasn't taken. And he went along anyway, out of loyalty, or shame, or not wanting his nephew to go alone. The epic doesn't say which. It just shows two good arguments losing to one sleepless man.
screen: `FATE AND EFFORT TOGETHER` · `ASK THE ELDERS FIRST` · `"THEY BROKE THE RULES FIRST"` · then, large: `THEY FOLLOW HIM ANYWAY`

Breathe in, and remember the words. Breathe out, and notice what you did next: stayed, left, went along. Don't grade yourself. Just see it. If you pray, you can bring that person into your prayer. The bell holds the time.

852.title: Sauptika: the night massacre
852.hook: a gigantic being blocks the gate of the sleeping camp, and every weapon Ashvatthama throws disappears into it
852.howItsDone: Hindus who worship Shiva as Mahadeva call on him by many names, and the hymn Ashvatthama offers at the gate is one of the places in the Mahabharata where those names are gathered.

segments.voice: Your line: Sauptika: the night massacre. Yesterday Kripa gave good counsel under the banyan, lost the argument, and followed his nephew anyway. Whose advice did you go and ask? Day eight hundred fifty-two.

The Pandava camp is dark and quiet. Ashvatthama reaches the gate with Kripa and Kritavarma behind him. And the gate isn't empty. Something is standing there, so large it seems to fill the night. In Ganguli's English it's a being of enormous size, terrible to look at, blazing, wrapped in a tiger skin, with snakes for ornaments and many eyes. It doesn't speak. It just stands between Ashvatthama and the sleeping camp. Today, what happens at the gate, and the strange offering Ashvatthama makes before he can go through.
screen: `THE CAMP IS ASLEEP.` → `A BEING AT THE GATE.` → `IT DOESN'T SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Ashvatthama does what a warrior does. He attacks. He hurls weapon after weapon at the being, and the being swallows them. Every one vanishes into it, and it stands there untouched. Now he's empty-handed, at night, in front of something he can't fight. And now the text lets him think about the advice he ignored. In effect, he says: whoever turns away from the counsel of friends who wish him well comes to grief, and that's what I've done. Then he turns to Mahadeva, the great god, Shiva. He praises him with many names. And an altar of gold appears in front of him, with a fire blazing on it, and fierce companions of Shiva crowd around. Ashvatthama offers the only thing he has left. He offers himself. He steps into the fire. Shiva appears, and the text has him speak plainly. He has protected the Panchalas until now, out of regard for Krishna. But their time is over. Then Shiva gives Ashvatthama a sword and enters into his body, and Ashvatthama rises from the fire blazing with that power. It's a hard scene, and the epic doesn't smooth it over. The gate held until a man gave himself up completely. What came through the gate afterward was no longer just Ashvatthama's anger. Shiva's own words say the sleeping camp's time had come. Tomorrow, what that means.
screen: `THE WEAPONS VANISH` · `"I IGNORED MY FRIENDS"` · `HE OFFERS HIMSELF` · then, large: `SHIVA ENTERS HIM`

segments.voice: Sit still and picture a doorway you know well, your front door or a door at work. Breathe in, and imagine standing on its threshold, not yet through. Breathe out, and stay there, unhurried. Bring to mind a moment when you ran out of your usual tools and had to stop. What did you reach for then? Stay with that question for a few breaths without answering it. If you pray, you can rest in prayer with open hands. The bell holds the time.

853.title: Sauptika: the night massacre
853.hook: a man wakes to a foot on his chest and asks for one thing, to die by a weapon, and is refused
853.howItsDone: Reciters of the Mahabharata tell the night attack as a story of grief and wrongdoing, and the death of Draupadi's sons leads into her demand for justice in the next part of the book.

segments.voice: Your line: Sauptika: the night massacre. Yesterday the being at the gate swallowed every weapon, and Ashvatthama offered himself to Shiva. When your usual way stopped working, what did you reach for? Day eight hundred fifty-three.

Dhrishtadyumna is asleep in his tent, on a fine bed, the commander of the Pandava army resting after the war he helped win. He is the man who killed Drona. He wakes because someone is standing on him. It's Ashvatthama, Drona's son. This is the night the whole book is named for, and the epic tells it without looking away. Today we'll tell it more gently, and hold on to the few moments the text slows down for: a request, a refusal, and a message brought to a dying king.
screen: `A COMMANDER ASLEEP.` → `DRONA'S SON STANDS OVER HIM.` → `THE NIGHT ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Dhrishtadyumna, pinned down, asks for one thing. In Ganguli's telling he begs Ashvatthama to kill him with a weapon, so that he dies as a warrior and reaches the worlds warriors reach. Ashvatthama refuses. A man who killed his teacher, he says in effect, doesn't deserve a warrior's death. And he kills him without a weapon. Then he moves through the camp. Others wake and fall: Shikhandi, Uttamaujas, Yudhamanyu, and the five young sons of Draupadi, who came to the war with their fathers. In the dark, people wake confused, some striking at each other. Outside, Kripa and Kritavarma stand at the gate and cut down those who flee, and fire is set to the camp. When it's over, the three go back across the field to Duryodhana, still lying where he fell, barely alive. They tell him what they've done. And the dying king answers, in effect, that they've done for him what Bhishma, Karna and Drona couldn't, and he dies. But there are names missing from that night. The five Pandava brothers aren't in the camp. Neither are Krishna or Satyaki. Earlier that evening, the text says, Krishna had taken them away to spend the night elsewhere. So the men Ashvatthama most wanted to strike were never there. The ones who died were the commander, the warriors, and Draupadi's sons. That's Sauptika: a vengeance that reaches everyone except its target.
screen: `A WARRIOR'S DEATH REFUSED` · `THROUGH THE SLEEPING CAMP` · `DURYODHANA HEARS AND DIES` · then, large: `THE PANDAVAS WEREN'T THERE`

854.title: Sauptika: the night massacre
854.hook: a mother sits down and refuses to eat until she sees the jewel from her sons' killer's head
854.howItsDone: Ashvatthama's wandering under Krishna's curse is told in retellings of the epic, and some Hindus tell stories of him still wandering the earth.

segments.voice: Your line: Sauptika: the night massacre. Yesterday the camp was struck in its sleep, Duryodhana died hearing of it, and the Pandavas weren't there. Who else did your anger nearly reach? Day eight hundred fifty-four.

Morning. Dhrishtadyumna's charioteer, one of the few who got away, brings the news to Yudhishthira, and the king falls to the ground. Then Draupadi comes. Her brother is dead. Her five sons are dead. She sits down in front of her husbands and says she'll take no food until Ashvatthama pays for this. And she names what she wants. Ashvatthama was born with a jewel on his head. She wants to see it brought back, and worn by Yudhishthira. Today, the end of the night book, and what happens to that jewel.

segments.voice: Bhima rides out at once. Krishna warns the others that Bhima is in danger: Drona once taught his son a weapon called Brahmashira, terrible enough to burn the worlds, and Ashvatthama is reckless enough to use it. So Krishna, Arjuna and Yudhishthira follow. They find Ashvatthama on the bank of the Ganga, sitting among sages with the sage Vyasa. When he sees them, he picks up a blade of grass, charges it as that weapon, and lets it go. Arjuna answers with the same weapon. Two fires rise to meet each other. And then two sages, Narada and Vyasa, step between the weapons to save the world. Arjuna, who has kept his vows, can call his weapon back, and he does. Ashvatthama can't. So he turns his toward the wombs of the Pandava women. Krishna answers that Uttara's child, the unborn son of Abhimanyu, will live, because Krishna himself will revive him. Then Krishna curses Ashvatthama: to wander the earth alone, sick, shunned, for a very long time. Ashvatthama gives up the jewel. They carry it back to Draupadi, and she hands it to Yudhishthira, and he wears it. This week opened in the shadow of a blow on a holy plain, and it closes with a jewel on a king's head. The night book ends with a grieving mother's demand met, and the next generation saved by one promise.
